items.title: Prinsjesdag 2026: 5 thema’s uitgelicht voor bibliotheken
items.raw_text: Prinsjesdag 2026 zit erop. De nieuw gepresenteerde plannen laten zien dat het kabinet vertrouwen heeft in de toekomst van bibliotheken. Er komt meer zekerheid voor leesbevordering, bibliotheken krijgen een belangrijke maatschappelijke rol en er is geld voor verdere ontwikkeling. Tegelijkertijd zijn er ook uitdagingen. Gaby Erckens, onze teamleider Financiën en Control, dook in de plannen en zette de belangrijkste 5 thema’s op een rij. 1. Structureel geld voor leesbevordering Goed nieuws is dat de programma’s BoekStart en de Bibliotheek op school vanaf 2027 structurele financiering krijgen. Dat betekent dat je als bibliotheek of school niet langer afhankelijk bent van tijdelijke subsidies. Voor 2027 is hiervoor €38 miljoen beschikbaar. Vanaf 2028 groeit dit naar €50 miljoen per jaar. Bibliotheken en scholen kunnen dus langdurige plannen maken en blijven investeren in leesplezier, taalontwikkeling en onderwijs. 2. Om gemeenten hierbij te ondersteunen, stelt het Rijk jaarlijks ongeveer € 60 miljoen beschikbaar. Ook kleinere gemeenten krijgen ondersteuning. Voor hen geldt een minimumbedrag van €100.000, zodat lokale bibliotheekvoorzieningen behouden blijven of opnieuw kunnen openen. Wat deze ontwikkeling laat zien? items.title: De grootste uitdaging zit niet in de technologie. We moeten het werk opnieuw ontwerpen.

Eind juni sprak Doeser tijdens een NDS-bijeenkomst in Oss, die was georganiseerd vanuit de prioriteit Digitaal Vakmanschap. items.title: Nederlanders denken dat ze phishing herkennen, maar AI maakt oplichting steeds echter en juist dát is een groot veiligheidsrisico
items.raw_text: Uit het jaarlijkse nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, mede mogelijk gemaakt door het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, blijkt dat Nederlanders wél weten wat veilig online gedrag is, maar gemiddeld slechts een derde van de veilige handelingen consequent toepassen. Den Haag – Nederlanders weten goed hoe ze zich online moeten beschermen, maar vertrouwen opvallend vaak op hun eigen vermogen om gevaar te herkennen. Zodra er meer van hen gevraagd wordt dan kijken, neemt de motivatie om zich veilig te gedragen af. Slechts één op de zes gebruikt altijd tweefactorauthenticatie, een dubbel slot voor je accounts en apparaten dat ervoor zorgt dat er meer nodig is dan een wachtwoord om in te loggen. Zo kunnen criminelen met een gestolen wachtwoord niet zomaar een account overnemen. En maar drie op de tien gaan altijd zelf naar de officiële website in plaats van op een link te klikken. items.raw_text: ECP-directeur Arie van Bellen ging in een recente aflevering van de podcastreeks ECP Talks in gesprek met ECP-programmaregisseur Sabine Herbrink over het programma Digitaal Doordacht. items.title: OTC Whitepaper Soevereiniteit
items.raw_text: Digitale soevereiniteit betekent niet dat organisaties alle digitale diensten zelf moeten bezitten of beheren. Het betekent dat zij aantoonbare grip hebben op kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden: inzicht in de keten, bewuste risicoacceptatie, uitvoerbare alternatieven, onafhankelijke controle en transparante communicatie over keuzes en restrisico’s. In het whitepaper over digitale soevereiniteit vertaalt de Online Trust Coalitie dit thema naar een praktisch handelingskader voor bestuurders, IT-verantwoordelijken, toezichthouders, serviceproviders en risk- en compliancefuncties. De OTC stelt dat digitale soevereiniteit niet draait om volledige autonomie of autarkie, maar om aantoonbare beheersing: inzicht in kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden, expliciete risicoafweging, uitvoerbare exit-mogelijkheden, onafhankelijke controle en heldere communicatie over restrisico’s en gemaakte keuzes. De OTC signaleert dat impliciet vertrouwen in digitale diensten onder druk staat. Geopolitieke spanningen, conflicterende rechtsstelsels, concentratie van leveranciersmacht en complexe beheerketens maken zichtbaar dat organisaties niet langer kunnen volstaan met contracten, certificaten of algemene toezeggingen. items.title: 🌐 🏢 IFLA MENA RDC & Bibliotheca Alexandrina Conclude Landmark Workshop on AI in Libraries 🤖 📚 ✨
items.raw_text: End of AI Workshop Group Photo The “Artificial Intelligence in Libraries” workshop, jointly organized by the IFLA Middle East and North Africa ( MENA ) Regional Division Committee and the Bibliotheca Alexandrina , has successfully concluded at the Library’s Multipurpose Hall on October 29 th 2026. The event brought together library professionals to address the growing role of emerging technologies in the field. Working in collaborative groups, participants drafted a preliminary practical framework for AI integration in libraries. The draft draws upon the Egyptian Supreme Council of Universities’ AI guide as well as international best practices and standards. In the coming weeks, participants will continue refining the document, with a strong focus on establishing a robust ethical framework for adoption of AI. To build on this momentum, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina and IFLA MENA will host follow-up events and training sessions over the coming months to expand the reach of the initiative and keep professionals abreast of key industry developments.

If you are interested in joining the Bibliography Section Standing Committee for a four-year term starting in August 2027, the first step is to submit an Expression of Interest between 28 October and 9 December 2026. Please note that this is the only window to express your interest during the 2027 election cycle. No nominator is required at this stage. The subsequent election stages are: 6 January – 17 February 2027: Nomination period. 3 – 31 March 2027: Voting period. We welcome colleagues with experience and an interest in national bibliographies, bibliographic standards, metadata, bibliographic control and related fields. For full details and instructions, please consult the IFLA announcement: Elections 2027 – Call for Expressions of Interest . We would be delighted to welcome new colleagues, perspectives and expertise to BIBS! For any questions, please contact Rehab Ouf , Chair of the IFLA Bibliography Section.

items.title: MetLib 2026 | Day 4: Resilience, Solidarity and Letters to the Future
items.raw_text: The final day of MetLib 2026 was perhaps the most emotional, bringing the conference’s discussions about resilience, community and the future of libraries into a deeply human perspective. In a moving opening keynote, Yuliya Vaganova, Director of the Khanenko Museum in Kyiv, Ukraine , shared the experience of keeping a cultural institution alive during wartime. Despite the destruction caused by the war, the museum continued to find ways to connect with its community through innovative programmes, some of which received European recognition. Among the most powerful examples were performances by a theatre group featuring actors with Down syndrome and a blood donation campaign — a reminder of how essential solidarity becomes in times of crisis. Looking towards the future, participants also took part in scenario-planning workshops , exploring possible futures and reflecting on how libraries might prepare for the challenges and opportunities ahead. One of the most personal moments of the conference was an invitation to write letters to the future . Throughout the event, participants had received messages written from the perspective of a fellow librarian living in the future. On the final day, they responded with handwritten letters of their own, sharing personal reflections, hopes and questions inspired by the conference. The organisers plan to publish these letters one by one in the coming months, extending the conversation beyond MetLib 2026. The conference concluded in Rotterda

items.title: Webinar: Selection and Collection of Statistical Data on Digital Libraries (Collections)
items.raw_text: Wednesday, November 4 | 16:00 – 17:30 CET Register to Attend Abstract Libraries are increasingly data-driven, but when it comes to digital collections, we still face a basic challenge: before we can measure consistently, we need to agree on what we are measuring. The “digital library” or “digital collection” can mean very different things to different institutions and professionals. Rather than aiming for a single standardized definition, today’s webinar is an opportunity to share perspectives, experiences, and approaches to collecting data about digital collections and their users. Our focus is on learning from one another and exploring the different ways we understand and work with these collections. We hope today’s discussion will help move the conversation forward. items.title: Authors Discuss Being Banned, Part 2: Malinda Lo, Ellen Hopkins, and Jennifer L. Armentrout
items.raw_text: The troubling trend of book challenges and bans in libraries across the US continues. In 2025, 4,235 titles were banned or challenged at public, school, or university libraries, according to the American Library Association’s (ALA) State of America’s Libraries 2026 report. This figure was the second highest (following the record set in 2023) since ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom (OIF) began documenting censorship attempts in 1990. Behind each title is an author being professionally—and sometimes personally—targeted for the stories they have chosen to share. These works usually amplify marginalized voices such as abuse victims or those within the LGBTQ+ community. American Libraries spoke with five authors on the Top 11 Most Challenged Books of 2025 list included in the report to hear how their experiences affected them. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.title: CBC Report: University Libraries are Being Swarmed by AI Bots, Putting Public Access at Risk
items.raw_text: From the CBC: University libraries say entire collections are being knocked offline by persistent streams of unruly bots trying to access their archives, which include academic, historical and government documents. “They’re just out there on the internet, just bombarding us with trying to grab up as much material as possible,” Jill Strykowski, cataloguing and government documents lead at San Jose State University, told CBC News. Eric Hellman, executive director of Project Gutenberg — a U.S.-based volunteer organization that digitizes and archives cultural works and distributes eBooks — wrote in a blog last year that these bots, which he characterizes as poorly programmed “monstrosities,” are “destroying open access” on the internet. He tells CBC News that “everything’s gotten worse” since he wrote that. [Clip] Some libraries have set up CAPTCHA challenges or other verification systems to weed out bots. The problem is, those measures can also weed out the good bots, says Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative academic initiative at NYU Law School and the University of Warwick focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions. Some libraries have also begun to require login credentials, a controversial move that those who spoke to CBC News say they want to avoid because it puts barriers on human access. While researchers are increasingly integrating AI into their research journeys, a recent survey conducted by OUP shows their trust in AI outputs remains low. This pilot aims to ensure high-quality, trusted content remains discoverable and responds to changing habits brought on by AI, such as the rise in zero-click search journeys. This collection surfaces the work taking place across open movements and highlights how practitioners and advocates can effectively collaborate for sustainable change. Open movements all center public access and broad representation, and work to prevent the concentration of power governing information and its monetization. As general discussion of openness has narrowed to focus on areas like open science, data, access, and education, these individual communities have grown distanced from each other and, occasionally, their shared values. items.title: Libraries Shaping AI Together
items.raw_text: When a group of Pottsboro, TX residents sat down at the library and asked ChatGPT, “Where can I send a fax in Pottsboro?” we hoped it would suggest the library. Instead, it told them to drive twelve miles to a mail store in another town. The question was part of a library workshop where residents tested what AI tools know, and don’t know, about our town. We expected that it might not know everything locals know. We did not expect it to send people to other towns to find services and activities available here. Being a tourist destination, it would be helpful for responses to include local restaurants, hotels, and fishing guides. That moment was on my mind when I went to Washington, DC, for the AI Civics convening hosted by Data & Society. AI Civics treats AI as part of civic life, something communities have a right to shape, not just a tool to learn. Our cohort is a mix of big city library systems, small town libraries like ours, and the National Digital Inclusion Alliance. Each of us is running our own pilot. Different Libraries, Same Questions It turns out a library serving a few hundred people and one serving tens of thousands have a lot in common. We keep running into the same questions. Who gets represented in AI? Who gets left out? Who gets a say? And there is no customer service number you can call to fix what ChatGPT says about your town. items.title: Scaffolding Early Literacy Learning During Public Library Storytime
items.raw_text: Public library storytimes are more than just a fun time for children; beneath the read-alouds, singing songs, fingerplays, bubbles, and movement activities, storytimes are packed with abundant opportunities that support children’s literacy learning [1]. We all know intentionality is a key ingredient to promote learning in storytime [2]. One way to do this is by incorporating the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) [3], an educational theory by Lev Vygotsky, into storytime planning and design. With a little bit of foreplanning, we can structure literacy experiences to align with children’s developmental levels—the perfect spot for learning—neither too easy nor too challenging. This article provides an introduction and practical tips for storytime providers on how to intentionally scaffold learning during picture book reading in storytime using the ZPD. The Zone of Proximal Development So what exactly is the Zone of Proximal Development? The ZPD, as explained by Vygotsky, is the gap between what children can do alone and what children can do with the guidance of more knowledgeable others (Vygotsky et al., 1978). Think of it as a linear continuum. There are three different learning levels. Imagine that at one end of the continuum is a task children can perform independently. At the other end of the continuum is a task children cannot perform, even with help. And in the middle of the continuum is the ZPD, in which children can perform the task with guidance and support. items.title: Erica Kent On The Light And Shadows Of Her Magnificent New Novel
items.raw_text: Reader’s first meet Jessica Ryder, the captivating protagonist of Erica Kent’s Black Dog , as a smart and brash eleven-year-old living with her alcoholic father in Brookline, Massachusetts. It’s 1980 and Jessica, an ardent music fan, is devastated over the death of John Lennon. In a misguided attempt to comfort her, Jessica’s father offers her a beer. This fateful act kicks off a near-decade long struggle with alcohol and drugs, which Kent depicts with clarity and empathy. Kent masterfully charts Jessica’s adolescence as the young woman negotiates her complicated family dynamic, not only with her father, but also with her mother and sister, who live in a far different socioeconomic world in nearby Boston. What follows is not only a riveting coming of age story but also a clear-eyed examination of the often fraught road to recovery. The reviews have been rapturous for Black Dog . items.title: E-Rate Under Threat: Take a Stand and Show Up for E-Rate
items.raw_text: After thirty years of keeping libraries online, the E-Rate program has seen its share of challenges. Just in the last two years, the program weathered the loss of support for hotspot lending and suffered through a Supreme Court Challenge . While the Supreme Court decision ultimately went in our favor, there is no time to sit back and relax for library advocates. In June, the Federal Communication’s Commission (FCC) launched a proceeding (officially, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking) that threatens to terminate this vital program. Now is the time to show up for E-Rate and tell the FCC what broadband access at your library means for your community. A Quick E-Rate Refresher One of four programs within the FCC’s Universal Service Fund, set up in the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the E-Rate program was established to ensure public libraries and K-12 schools have affordable access to advanced telecommunications (i.e., broadband and internet access). Today, E-Rate provides funding to almost three-quarters of public libraries to help offset monthly internet service costs and the costs for eligible technology necessary for making sure Wi-Fi is available throughout the building. How much are we talking about? Currently the program sends about $2.4 billion to public libraries and K-12 schools annually. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. Adaptive books may include page extenders, symbol-supported text, tactile features, or other modifications that support engagement and independence. What struck me most was that
